Let me tell you the story behind these numbers. Before Penang, our on-time delivery rate had been sliding for two quarters, from ninety-six to ninety-one percent, and nobody had noticed, because the slide was slow. Then, in June, while we were still relying on a single plant, the fire hit, and the rate bottomed out at eighty-four percent. That was our outlier month. By the time we launched the Monterrey pilot in July, clients had been waiting an average of eleven days for keyboards. Here is what happened next. The rate climbed for eight weeks and then leveled off at ninety-seven percent, which is above our old baseline. Year over year, that is a gain of three points. One number skews the picture: freight costs spiked in August, while we were moving stock between the two sites. If we drill down, that spike was a one-time cost. The trajectory is clear. We had been running on a single point of failure for years, and we have finally fixed it.

Hi Fabiana, Marcus here. The board review just ended, and I wanted to call while it's fresh. The chart was good, but the story was better. When you said the rate had been sliding for two quarters before anyone noticed, you could see the chairman sit up. That one line did more than any slide. Two questions came up after you left. First, the CFO wants to know whether the freight spike could happen again, so please send him the drill-down by Friday. Second, someone asked what our baseline will be next year. I said ninety-seven percent, but let's agree on that before I repeat it. One small note: at one point you were reading the numbers off the slide. Next time, tell them the trajectory first and let the chart confirm it. Great job. They have approved the second supplier for all hardware.
